model.transport: fresh isolated tool-enabled agent; tools only read prompts and serialize explicit judgments
model.blinding: procedural file-access restrictions, not an operating-system access guarantee

rows.text:
Let readers choose among the afternoons and collection times they can manage, ranking those options on their request sheets. Staff should consider the sheets together before allocating shelf space. Two readers with the same first choice may both be happy with appointments that bring them in at different times. Record each booking under the reader’s name with the title requested. Their message that they are setting out is the cue to prepare the title from that list. This lets someone book well ahead without drawing a helper away from people collecting now.

Allocate each book a place on whichever shelf has space. Write the spot on the desk list next to the name and appointment time, so either piece of information will lead staff to it. For a missed collection, offer the reader a choice of times still available. Once they choose, move the book and book the additional period that was being held for them.

People taking a seat should find the quiet-waiting notice there when the doors open. A helper can welcome several arrivals, record their names and carry the sheet to the desk at intervals. At the greeting, ask each person whether they would like help finding or carrying anything and record the help they choose. Use the wait to deal with everyday questions. A helper can ask what people need to know and write the answers on the question pad, so readers are ready when called.

Work the collection desk in short periods. As each begins, check the waits for people with appointments and those without, then serve the group that has waited longer first. In this way a lengthening walk-in queue gets attention too. Send a written account of who is present to the helpers preparing books. They can fill the delivery tray with titles for those people. If service runs late, staff should speak to the affected readers while a helper changes the public notice. On the way out, a helper can hand readers a comment card and show them where to drop it, freeing the desk for collections.

Set aside a place for people to leave returns with a slip they fill out themselves. They can go once they have left their books. Helpers use the slips to inspect the books in the order received. As soon as a few have been checked, put them on the trolley in shelf order so a single quick trip puts them back in use.

An outgoing helper should make a list of unfinished work before the relief helper arrives. While both are there, go over the list together. To plan the following afternoon, use the closing review to identify the worst delays in the log. Read the comments about those particular stages and choose one change based on readers’ experiences there.

rows.text:
Take requests to borrow cups from guests as they stand in line for drinks. A volunteer can fill in the cards as they go and take them to the drinks counter and the cup station, keeping both teams informed while guests hold their places. If there are fewer clean cups than requests, find out when each guest expects to use the cup. Serve the soonest need first. Someone who only needs theirs for a later session can get one from the next lot.

Display the map of return points on the counter so guests can check it before picking a cup. Keep pocket copies beside the cups too. The volunteer lending a cup should note what makes it recognizable and ask the borrower to enter the time they intend to return it. Letting guests set that time gives them a part in the agreement. Ask there and then what would help them return it, and relay the answers immediately to those staffing the return points so they can act during this round of loans. A borrower who needs an extension can explain how much longer they need, agree on a revised time with a volunteer and have the volunteer record it.

For a short spell at a busy drop-off, have two volunteers work alongside each other. The first takes cups from guests, looks them over and sets them in a washable crate, at which point guests are free to go. The second looks after the loan register. Once a small crate has filled, that volunteer can match the cups to their descriptions and check them off in one sitting while the first keeps receiving returns.

An entry on the transfer list signals that a crate is ready for a volunteer to carry to the nearby wash station. This keeps the crates moving at the rate they fill. After washing the cups as usual, the washer should add them to the clean stock tally before taking them over to lending. The lending volunteers can then get ready for the next guests they have cups for. When supplies run low, split the work between someone updating the stock notice and someone reviewing requests with the people waiting. If loans have fallen overdue, carry a reminder sign on a circuit of the drop-off points. Then post the outstanding count on the announcement board. Guests see the reminder somewhere they can return a cup, and volunteers have no need to retain contact information.

Allow a few minutes for the two shifts to work together. As each duty changes hands, both teams should amend the handover note to show who now has it. Once the last returns have been counted, divide the spares between the lending station and the reserve shelf. Base the split on how long the coming periods of service should last and keep the opening period’s supply within reach. For the next improvement, take the most frequent guest comment and check it against lending totals and actual return times. Choose a change that tackles a problem borne out by those records.

rows.text:
The coordinator can get sign-ups going by putting possible garden sessions on the calendar. Volunteers signing up later will see the same choices as the first arrivals, and they can indicate when even a brief visit is possible. For routine work still without an owner, have the coordinator make provisional assignments on the board, allowing for the effort each job will take. People can then trade to find a better fit while keeping every job covered. Anyone who needs to change a visit should correct the calendar and then flag the affected work on the board for others to see.

Walk the beds and share the findings on the board before opening watering jobs for sign-up. Everyone choosing a job can then apply the agreed watering advice to the same observations. File the garden notes by day, using a page for each date and identifying each bed visited with its own observations. That will allow someone to compare beds as they were on the same day. Break seedling care into short shifts and offer them first for volunteers with experience to choose. The coordinator can do the remaining shifts or arrange cover, leaving most people with times of their own choosing.

Post compost turning as a two-person session with two visible spaces for names. Either one is open to any volunteer, and a single name shows others that person still needs company. Someone learning a regular task can start by reading its card and doing the work. They can ask an experienced volunteer to look it over afterward and demonstrate a correction while they still remember the attempt.

Keep requests for tools on a list at the storage area. If a tool is out, whoever has it can agree on a return time with the next volunteer so the latter can plan their work. When several jobs need materials, bring the volunteers together to discuss the work and the amounts each requires. Once they have settled the shares, submit one combined quantity. Gardeners who will briefly be away from a shared plot should leave a list of the care they would like. Others can choose a job knowing they have the regular gardeners’ backing.

Find out from neighbors when they could collect produce, then divide what is ready among those collection times. A host welcoming newcomers can give them the map and let them locate the common paths, work areas and meeting places, answering questions if something is hard to find. Observe when the different paths are in use and reserve quiet periods for small maintenance jobs so visitors have access when traffic is heaviest.

For the shared bed meeting, have each member offer one idea and explain its purpose. Combine ideas with compatible aims into a single planting plan. When members discuss the season, invite them to propose a priority. Weigh the suggestion against the observations of the beds and the attendance record before choosing, so the priority suits both growing conditions and the time people have been able to contribute.

rows.text:
Arrange a group booking in a single conversation between the organizer and museum staff. Work out what the group would enjoy, which rooms it can visit and when a volunteer can accompany it, allowing both parties to revise the arrangements as they talk. Divide weekend service into short periods with a dedicated reception volunteer and a dedicated interpreter for the whole of each period. Visitors can find someone for directions on arrival, and anyone discussing a work can stay with the volunteer who began the conversation.

Ask a new arrival what they are interested in, then show them a suitable first room on the map. With a repeat visitor, find out which room stood out on their previous visit. Point them toward a related object in a room that will be new to them. If time is tight, let the visitor choose appealing highlights on the guide sheet first. Use the estimated viewing times to help narrow the list around their favorites.

Try a suitable route from the map with a small party. After it has gone through, ask the room volunteers about crowding and decide whether the next party should follow it. Do that again for every group so the suggested routes reflect conditions in the galleries. A guide leading a tour should arrive with a short themed itinerary. Before the group departs, describe it and adapt it to what the visitors say they would most like to linger over.

Invite visitors to compare pieces in different locations by repeating a question on each piece’s label. Save the explanation of the connection for a label at the end, giving people time to form their own ideas. For an object associated with a local story, place the account before the encounter with the object and a question for reflection after it. People can then look for details they have just read about. Design the folded activity sheet for independent visitors so they look closely at the piece first. Unfolding the sheet reveals the writing prompt once they have had a chance to notice details for themselves.

When a group pauses to talk, the room volunteer should lead with a question. After people have discussed it, ask them to put any questions the exchange suggested on cards. At a display that brings back memories, allow time to write a recollection on a card and leave it at the exhibit. The writer can choose whether to share it in conversation with a volunteer. For other feedback, include the visitor route on the comment card and let people mark where something held their attention so the team can place their account.

Near closing time, one volunteer should update the time left on the reception display while others give reminders in the rooms. To improve a description, try revised text on display and keep track of questions that recur once it is in place. These point to explanations visitors still need. Bring one modest proposed change to the weekend review. Consider what room attendance, visitor feedback and the volunteers’ firsthand observations each suggest would happen in a trial, and look for agreement across the three before deciding to go ahead.

evidence.decision_a52c0a61ba2b:
If time is tight, let the visitor choose appealing highlights on the guide sheet first.
Use the estimated viewing times to help narrow the list around their favorites.
evidence.decision_e574ca310618:
With a repeat visitor, find out which room stood out on their previous visit.
Point them toward a related object in a room that will be new to them.
evidence.decision_afed3418c84e: For other feedback, include the visitor route on the comment card and let people mark where something held their attention so the team can place their account.
evidence.decision_896834903e5b:
To improve a description, try revised text on display and keep track of questions that recur once it is in place.
These point to explanations visitors still need.
evidence.decision_93f87b72b73f:
At a display that brings back memories, allow time to write a recollection on a card and leave it at the exhibit.
The writer can choose whether to share it in conversation with a volunteer.
evidence.decision_ce7fdbc55099:
Divide weekend service into short periods with a dedicated reception volunteer and a dedicated interpreter for the whole of each period.
Visitors can find someone for directions on arrival, and anyone discussing a work can stay with the volunteer who began the conversation.
evidence.decision_bbe43118a354:
For an object associated with a local story, place the account before the encounter with the object and a question for reflection after it.
People can then look for details they have just read about.
evidence.decision_095faae08d2f: Ask a new arrival what they are interested in, then show them a suitable first room on the map.
evidence.decision_954b40fc1668:
Invite visitors to compare pieces in different locations by repeating a question on each piece’s label.
Save the explanation of the connection for a label at the end, giving people time to form their own ideas.
evidence.decision_47bd37ecde77: Near closing time, one volunteer should update the time left on the reception display while others give reminders in the rooms.

decision_109bee88f2c1.text: Arrange a group booking in a single conversation between the organizer and museum staff.
Work out what the group would enjoy, which rooms it can visit and when a volunteer can accompany it, allowing both parties to revise the arrangements as they talk.

decision_034dcf8498b0.text: Try a suitable route from the map with a small party.
After it has gone through, ask the room volunteers about crowding and decide whether the next party should follow it.
Do that again for every group so the suggested routes reflect conditions in the galleries.

decision_d069333dcdbb.text: When a group pauses to talk, the room volunteer should lead with a question.
After people have discussed it, ask them to put any questions the exchange suggested on cards.

decision_e1233fe46483.text: Bring one modest proposed change to the weekend review.
Consider what room attendance, visitor feedback and the volunteers’ firsthand observations each suggest would happen in a trial, and look for agreement across the three before deciding to go ahead.

decision_2435ae99c474.text: Design the folded activity sheet for independent visitors so they look closely at the piece first.
Unfolding the sheet reveals the writing prompt once they have had a chance to notice details for themselves.
